head:
Society · Fitness of young adults

Unfit before adulthood: when the army can no longer find recruits

Before signing a contract, an army needs to know whether a young body will hold up. So it measures the weight, health, fitness and school level of a very large number of candidates, and sometimes publishes what it finds. It is an indicator that does not come from sport. This article reads it closely: it separates what belongs to physical fitness from what does not, then looks at what the American, Swiss, French and Austrian armies say.

The problem

You may have already seen this sentence: “77% of 17-24 year olds would be unfit for military service”. It has been circulating since September 2022, with the implied idea that young people are in poor shape. The figure does exist: it comes from a US Department of Defense study, confirmed to the press by a Pentagon spokesperson.1,2 But it does not say what it is made to say. In this study, “unfit” covers seven criteria: weight, illnesses, mental health, drugs, criminal record, dependants and school level. A performance measured under effort is not one of them.1

Why stop at it, if it is a military matter? Because the army is one of the few institutions with a direct interest in knowing whether young adults can produce an effort. When it is short of recruits, it looks at its own data, including real fitness tests taken by hundreds of thousands of young people. This thermometer comes neither from a gym nor from a brand. You just have to learn to read it.

So the question comes in two parts. First, what exactly is being measured when a young person is called “unfit”? Then, when physical condition is actually measured, in Switzerland, in France, in Austria, what do we find, and what does it change for you?

The question

When armies say that many young people are unfit, how much of that finding really comes down to physical fitness, and what do the fitness tests themselves show about the condition of young adults?

We proceed in six steps, from the most general to the most precise: the American figure, the accumulation of reasons, the sorting between physical fitness and the rest, the change since 2013, fitness tests in Europe, then the objections.

What is at stake

For the US Army, the stake is first of all numerical. In 2018, it missed its target of 70,000 recruits by 6,500.3 In 2022, it aimed for 485,000 active-duty soldiers and counted 466,000.4 Physical fitness is only one cause among others, but it is costly once recruits have arrived. In a study by the Army Public Health Center and its partners of 99,335 recruits who entered training in 2017, 33,509 (about one third) had at least one musculoskeletal injury, for more than 14.8 million dollars in medical costs. About 62% of the women were affected, and 32% of the men.5

For you, the stake is more concrete. If you are aiming for a job with physical tests (army, gendarmerie, fire brigade), you will be rejected or admitted on criteria you know little about. You can fail for a reason of weight, health, fitness test or something else, and the remedies differ. Confusing these cases means putting your effort in the wrong place.

There is also a stake in how the figure is read. A misunderstood figure produces either panic (“a whole generation is lost”) or denial (“it is propaganda”). Neither reaction helps you decide. Finally, a thermometer that captures 17-24 year olds makes it possible to spot early what is changing in the condition of a generation, provided you do not make it say more than it measures.
rest:
Step 1 of 6 · The starting figure

The 77% figure exists, but it is an eligibility estimate, not a finding about fitness

The primary source is the 2020 “Qualified Military Available” (QMA) study, a Department of Defense technical report dated March 2022, accompanied by a presentation from April 2022.1,6 It covers 32,878,937 young people aged 17 to 24. Those who can enlist without a waiver are 23% (7,617,383 young people), against 29% in the 2013 version of the same model. The remaining 77% are the young people who cannot enlist “without a waiver”, that is, without a service granting an exception.6 The document does not say more about what a waiver is.

Two points on the nature of the figure. It is not a census: it is an estimate produced by a statistical model, calibrated on health surveys (NHANES 2015-2018, NSDUH 2019), a Department survey of young people and 2.4 million applicant records.1 Second, “unfit” is a misleading translation: the authors write “disqualified without a waiver”, an administrative status.

The great majority of young people ruled out are ruled out for more than one criterion at once

One dot = 1 young person in 100, aged 17-24, United States, estimate for 2020. A single criterion: 33% (11 + 8 + 7 + 4 + 1 + 1 + 1). Source: Department of Defense, QMA 2020.1,6

What this means

The 77% breaks down as 33 + 44. Four ruled-out young people in seven (44 out of 77, derived) are ruled out by several criteria, not by a single one. So if everyone’s weight could be “fixed”, 77% would not go down to 23%.

The study goes further: among the 23% who are eligible, some are in education. The “available” for the army (eligible and not at university) are only 12% (4,062,307 young people), of whom 7% with the best aptitude test scores.6 It is this 12%, not the 23%, that represents the real pool.

The press picked up the figure, and a Pentagon spokesperson confirmed it to Military.com.2,7,8 But in the articles read, nobody distinguishes the criteria. Yet the biggest block of the chart, the 44 “several criteria” dots, is the one that is talked about least.

Step 2 of 6 · How the reasons add up

Most of the young people ruled out are ruled out for several reasons at once

For each criterion, the technical report gives the share of young people affected, alone or with others, from different surveys (NHANES for weight and illnesses, NSDUH for mental health and drugs).1 The April 2022 presentation gives the share of young people blocked by one criterion only. The two series complement each other.

One young person in three is overweight in the model’s terms, but very few are blocked by that criterion alone

Grey: blocked by that criterion alone (presentation). Colour: affected by that criterion, alone or combined (technical report). Aptitude is about 9% by construction (percentiles 1 to 9 of the AFQT test). Source: Department of Defense, QMA 2020.1,6

What this means

Take overweight. According to the model, about 35.4% of 17-24 year olds exceed a BMI of 27.5. Yet only 11% of young people are ruled out for that reason and nothing else. The calculation (11 out of 35.4, or about 31%, derived) indicates that nearly 7 overweight young people in 10 have at least one other ground of ineligibility.

Another derived calculation: the sum of the “affected” shares is 145.7%, or about 1.9 criteria per young person ruled out (145.7 out of 77). A young person who is ruled out has on average nearly two obstacles. The criteria are not independent: the study estimates their correlations.1

This applies to the weight figures you will come across elsewhere: “31% too heavy to serve” (Mission: Readiness, 2018), “27%” (press release from The Citadel university, 2018), 35.4% (2020 technical report). Neither the years nor necessarily the definitions are the same, and the article read on the 2018 report does not define obesity.3,9 Do not compare them with each other.

What remains is to see what each criterion measures, which will tell what, within the 77%, comes down to fitness.

Step 3 of 6 · What comes down to physical fitness

What comes down to physical fitness, and what does not

The technical report defines each criterion precisely.1 They can be sorted by asking: does it measure the ability to produce an effort?

CriterionHow it is measuredLink with fitness
OverweightBMI above 27.5, used as a substitute for fat mass (the armies then apply a body-fat threshold: more than 26% for men, more than 36% for women).Indirect: body composition, not performance
Medical / physicalAt least one of 17 NHANES conditions: anaemia, asthma, cancer, diabetes, hearing, hypertension, vision, etc.Health: some conditions may limit effort, none measures it
Drugs or alcoholCannabis in the last 30 days, any illicit drug, or dependence criteria.None
Mental healthSevere psychological distress over 12 months, or specialist care for a diagnosed disorder.None
ConductA judicial measure, two or more misdemeanours, or at least one felony.None
DependantsDependent children: the report cites married people with more than two children and those who declare at least one child.None
School aptitudeAFQT test: category V (percentiles 1 to 9) excluded.None

Of the seven criteria, two concern the body, and only one of them directly: weight. None measures a young person’s endurance, strength or power. Physical fitness in the strict sense appears nowhere in the study.

What this means

The “77%” is an eligibility figure, not a physical fitness figure. Of these 77 points, 18 (11 + 7, derived sum) are ruled out solely for a criterion concerning the body. The 44 “several criteria” points probably contain some of them, without the study quantifying it.

Fitness may play a role, but this figure cannot be used to measure it.

The US Army itself tested the idea that weight is not enough to tell fitness. In a 2009 study, 1,146 recruits above the weight or body-fat limits, but who had passed a physical test (five minutes of step climbing, one minute of push-ups), were compared with 10,514 compliant recruits. At 180 days, their risk of dropping out was not statistically different: risk ratio of 1.23 for men (interval from 0.95 to 1.58) and 1.17 for women (0.83 to 1.65). The intervals contain 1: no difference can be concluded.10 Since 2022, the Army has also offered a preparatory course to candidates 2 to 6 points of body fat above the standard, or with too low a school score.11

France has the same mix. The only mass result from the Journée défense et citoyenneté (defence and citizenship day) that we have read concerns reading: 13% with difficulties in 2024 among 843,500 young people tested.12 Here too, the school component has nothing to do with fitness. The French figures on fitness come from elsewhere, in step 5.

Step 4 of 6 · What has changed since 2013

What has changed since 2013 is mainly the accumulation of criteria

The same model was applied in 2013 and in 2020. The share of young people eligible without a waiver went from 29% to 23%. The authors write that this drop “is not the result of changes in the aptitude of young people, but rather an increase in other grounds for disqualification”. They specify that the 2013 model is not comparable with earlier ones.1,6

The biggest movement comes from young people with several obstacles at once

Change in percentage points between the 2013 model and the 2020 model; in brackets, the 2013 then 2020 values. Values rounded by the source: the changes in the reason rows do not add up exactly to the 6 points of the eligible. Source: Department of Defense, QMA 2020.6

What this means

The 6-point drop in the eligible comes mainly from the 5 extra points of young people with several grounds at once. Among the single criteria, mental health doubles (2% to 4%), overweight alone gains 1 point, school aptitude falls. Isolated overweight therefore does not explain the drop.

But be careful: a young person counted under “several criteria” may be overweight. Overweight may therefore contribute to the accumulation without the chart showing it. The study read does not detail the combinations.

The US Army’s article on its preparatory course attributes the deterioration to the pandemic, citing falling test scores and rising obesity.11 This explanation remains a hypothesis: none of the documents read demonstrates it. To know whether physical condition has really deteriorated, you have to leave the eligibility criteria and look at fitness tests, which is what the armies of Europe do.

Step 5 of 6 · The fitness tests themselves

When fitness itself is measured, the decline exists but it is modest

In Switzerland: a fitness test taken by almost all young men

In Switzerland, almost all young men go through recruitment and are tested there. In September 2026, the Federal Office of Sport announced a study published in BMJ Open, carried out with the army and the University of Zurich, on about 700,000 conscripts and volunteers tested between 2006 and 2024.13,14 The army’s fitness test has five events: progressive endurance, core strength, standing long jump, heavy ball throw, one-leg balance, each scored out of 25, so 125 points at most.15

Men score lower than before, but say they are more trained

Swiss conscripts and volunteers, 2006 to 2024. Mean army fitness test score (out of 125) and share of those who declare themselves “trained”. The women are volunteers, probably more motivated by sport than women as a whole. Source: Federal Office of Sport, press release of 8 September 2026 (the BMJ Open article was not read).13,14

What this means

The men’s mean score goes from 74.2 to 70.4 out of 125, that is 3.8 points or about 5% (derived calculation). The score of the female volunteers rises, from 45.4 to 49.9. At the same time, the share of men who consider themselves “trained” goes from 40% to 56%, 16 points more (derived): people see themselves as fitter than the test measures.

The authors put forward three partial explanations: the raising of the average recruitment age since the 2018 reform (the youngest score better), Covid restrictions, and popular sports that train core strength, basic endurance and balance less than the test does. They also note that everyone tends to overestimate their own activity.13

A second Swiss study shows where the decline is concentrated: 412,186 young men aged 18 to 23 recruited from 2007 to 2022, split into three groups by BMI, with a five-event score close to the previous one (maximum 125).16

The higher the BMI, the lower the fitness score

Adjusted mean score in the Swiss conscripts’ physical fitness test, 2007 to 2022. The gap of 19 points (73.6 minus 54.7) is a derived calculation. BMI can wrongly classify very muscular people. Source: Gubelmann et al., Preventive Medicine Reports, 2024.16

What this means

Young people with obesity score about 19 points lower than young people of normal weight, and those who are overweight about 7 points lower (73.6 minus 66.5, derived). The overweight and obesity groups represent about 20% and 5% of the sample (derived).

Over the period, the score of young people of normal weight changed by less than one point, whereas the overweight and obesity groups lost about 3 points. The authors note that the BMI of this population remained stable. This study and the previous one do not cover the same years or the same adjustments: their figures cannot be added together.16

In France: fitness for service that is deteriorating, but mixes the medical and the physical

In what we have read, there is no French equivalent of the Swiss test published on a large scale. The best benchmark is a Senate report of July 2019 on the Army (land forces). It follows, between 2011 and 2016, what happened to candidates who took the selection tests.17

Among candidates for the Army (land forces), the share of those immediately fit has fallen

Candidates who took the Army (land forces) selection tests, 2011 and 2016. The three percentages for 2011 total 101.8% in the text of the report: I reproduce them as they are. Source: Senate, information report no. 652, 2019.17,18

What this means

The share of immediately fit candidates goes from 83% to 76.3%, which is 6.7 points fewer (derived). Temporary unfitness goes from 14.2% to 18.4%, permanent unfitness from 4.6% to 5.6%. A temporary unfitness can be lifted: it is the share on which a candidate can act.

The report cites the High Committee for the Evaluation of the Military Condition: “the level of physical fitness of the recruitment pool is deteriorating”. It also reports a decline in success at written and sports tests, without quantifying it. Fitness for service, here, remains first of all medical: a physician’s thesis on 435 candidate files for the Foreign Legion, in 2022, finds 14% unfit, with dental lesions, visual disorders and orthopaedic disorders of the lower limb as frequent findings.17,19

For the Air Force, the same report gives, in 2017, 38.3% of candidates lost between summons and selection: 10.5% absent, 21.7% medically unfit and 6.1% withdrawals.17 More than one summoned candidate in five is therefore ruled out for a medical reason. In Austria, of 45,565 young men examined in 2023, 31,516 were declared fit (69.2%, derived, against 70.0% in 2022) and 9,989 unfit (21.9%). The Defence Minister cited the lack of physical fitness, especially overweight, and psychological fragility, without quantifying them separately.20

A pattern emerges: a real but measured decline, criteria that mix, a gap between feeling and measurement. It remains to see what these results do not allow us to conclude.

Step 6 of 6 · The objections

What these figures do not allow us to conclude

Four serious objections arise, and each has a partial answer.

Objection 1: “77% of young people unfit, so the army will never find recruits”

No, because the figure counts eligibility, not willingness. The study does not take into account the propensity to enlist. An October 2021 note from the Department’s JAMRS programme, cited in the presentation, estimates that increasing that propensity would expand the eligible and interested population by about 8.6%, against about 1.4% for relaxing several criteria (basis not specified).6 The Army missed its targets in 2022 and 2023, then reportedly reached the 2025 one four months early, without lowering its standards: this information comes from a specialist site with no author or date, to be taken with caution.4,21 The bottleneck is therefore not only physiological.

The preparatory course also shows the limits of a quick catch-up. In the 2022 pilot, 58 of the 97 trainees on the “fitness” track (about 60%, derived) reached the body-fat standard after two weeks. An officer cited by Army Times warns that all of this will “atrophy” if the lifestyle does not change.22 The sample is small, and the Army says so.

Objection 2: “young people’s physical condition is collapsing everywhere, and it keeps going”

Worldwide data add nuance. An analysis of 965,264 children and adolescents aged 9 to 17, in 19 high-income or upper-middle-income countries, finds a decline in cardiorespiratory fitness of 3.3 mL/kg/min, or 7.3%, between 1981 and 2014. This decline slowed in each decade and levelled off around 2000. It is stronger in boys and associated with rising income inequality.23,24 A figure you may have seen, “25% less physical capacity in forty years”, is attributed by the Fédération française de cardiologie to this work, with no test named: I did not find it again and I am not using it.25

Objection 3: “the Swiss figures prove that young people today are less fit”

They show that Swiss conscripts score a little lower than before, but the recruitment age and Covid explain part of the decline, and the female volunteers are improving. These Swiss tests say nothing about France or about causes: the mechanisms often mentioned (popular sports, screens, physical education) are not tested here.13

Objection 4: “weight is enough to judge fitness”

The Swiss data show a clear link between BMI and score. But the Swiss study notes that BMI can wrongly classify muscular people, and the 2009 American study shows that recruits above the limits pass a physical test and last as long as the others. Weight is a crude indicator; a fitness test is a direct indicator, with its own margin of error.10,16

The answer to the problem

How much of the finding “many young people are unfit” comes down to physical fitness? A much smaller share than the headline suggests. The 77% figure is real, but it is an administrative eligibility figure produced by a model. Of its seven criteria, only one comes close to physical condition, and only through weight. Four ruled-out young people in seven are ruled out by several criteria at once, mixing health, weight, habits and schooling. That is the most solid part.

What do fitness tests show about young adults? A modest but real decline among Swiss men (about 5% fewer points between 2006 and 2024), more marked among young people who are overweight or obese. In France, the fitness for service of Army (land forces) candidates fell between 2011 and 2016, with a significant medical share. Worldwide, the decline in children’s fitness levelled off around 2000. It is probable, but not demonstrated on a large scale: the tests differ from one country to another, part of the Swiss decline is due to recruitment age, and we found no French measure of fitness across all young people.

What remains unestablished: the causes. No study read shows why young people are less fit, or that recruitment depends mainly on fitness.

To remember: young people are ruled out for a mix of reasons, and many believe they are fitter than the tests show. In both cases, measuring is better than assuming.

What to put in place

The following actions are ordered. The retest frequency is an editorial choice, not a study finding, and none of these actions comes from a trial proving an effect on recruitment.

  1. Measure your fitness rather than assuming it.Take the test on this page. In Switzerland, 56% of conscripts say they are trained while their scores are falling: how you feel is not a measurement.13 Compare yourself with the test’s benchmarks rather than with your impression.
  2. Do not settle for weight.A BMI within the norm says nothing about your endurance, and a high BMI does not say either that you will fail a test.10,16 If you are aiming for an army corps or the gendarmerie, check the fitness-for-service conditions it publishes: they are not all physical, and some (medical) are settled by a medical opinion, not by training.
  3. Work on all the qualities tested, not just your usual sport.The Swiss test covers five qualities: endurance, core strength, jumping, throwing and balance. Its authors point out that popular sports train core strength, basic endurance and balance less.13,15 So add to your usual practice some work on what it leaves aside.
  4. Aim for regular practice, not a one-off effort.The Swiss report classes as “trained” those who do intense activity at least 3 times a week, for 20 minutes or more: a category definition, not a health prescription.15 And the gain from a course of a few weeks disappears if the lifestyle does not change.22
  5. Retest every 8 to 12 weeks, in the same conditions.Same place, same time, same warm-up: a difference smaller than the test’s margin of error proves nothing. Once a year is enough to monitor your trend.

A very low score, chest pain or abnormal breathlessness justify medical advice before you train harder.

What these figures do not say
  • The 77% figure comes from a statistical model on young Americans, calibrated on several surveys whose age ranges differ slightly (drugs and mental health cover 17-25 year olds).1
  • Candidates and volunteers do not represent all young people: they have already come forward.13,19
  • No large-scale French fitness test was found. The Austrian figures come from the press relaying the army, and the Swiss BMJ Open study was read only through its press release.13,20

Frequently asked questions

Are 77% of young people in poor physical shape?

No. This American figure measures eligibility without a waiver according to seven criteria, only one of which comes close to fitness (weight). Four ruled-out young people in seven are ruled out by several criteria at once.1,6

Are young French people less fit than before?

We have no national French measure. For the Army (land forces), the share of immediately fit candidates went from 83% to 76.3% between 2011 and 2016, with a significant medical share.17

Do you have to be slim to pass a fitness test?

A high BMI goes with a lower score on average among Swiss conscripts, but that is only an average.16
